title: Odile and the Colony
premise: Beatrix Vane has spent eleven years alone tending Relay Station Halcyon, the beacon that guides a generation ship's cryosleeping colonists toward a distant world. When the colony's children begin dreaming in unison of a woman in a glass tower, Beatrix discovers the beacon is not transmitting navigation data at all — it is broadcasting a dream, seeded by the station's original architect, her estranged mother, to choose which half of humanity the failing ship can wake and land. As the children's shared dream begins rewriting their waking minds, Beatrix must decode her mother's inheritance, fall in love with Ilya, the dream-touched boy who grew up inside her signal, and finally choose between saving the colonists' bodies or their capacity to love. In the end she splits the difference: she rewrites the beacon so half sleep on, dreaming, while the other half wakes — and she becomes the bridge between them, no longer alone.
about_author: Cyrus Whitlock is a former radio astronomer who left observatory life to write fiction about machines that outlive their makers. He lives off-grid in the Scottish Highlands, where he still maintains one very old antenna.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Glass Tower
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Routine maintenance on Relay Station Halcyon; we learn her isolation, her rituals, and the beacon nobody remembers commissioning. She logs an anomalous power draw she cannot explain. Emotional beat: loneliness worn smooth into habit, disturbed by the first crack of mystery.

chapters.title: Children of the Long Sleep
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV, aboard the colony ship Meridian. The children wake from cryo-dreams all describing the same woman in a tower of glass. Adults dismiss it as cryo-sickness. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into fear as the dream spreads night after night.

chapters.title: Signal Ghost
chapters.summary: Beatrix traces the anomaly to a buried sub-basement her schematics don't show — a second transmitter, older than the station itself, warm and running. Emotional beat: the uncanny intimacy of finding someone else's fingerprints on your solitude.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Says
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. The children begin speaking fragments of a language none were taught; Ilya dreams of Beatrix's face before he knows it exists. Emotional beat: the dream becoming identity, the first ache of longing for someone unreachable.

chapters.title: Mother's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Beatrix finds encrypted files signed E. Vane — her mother, who vanished when Beatrix was nine. The beacon is a message, and a machine for choosing. Emotional beat: grief reopened, anger at being made an instrument of an absent parent.

chapters.title: The Meridian Answers
chapters.summary: Beatrix hails the colony ship against protocol; instead of an officer, Ilya answers, having hijacked the comms console through his dream-knowledge. Their first conversation. Emotional beat: two solitudes recognizing each other across the dark.

chapters.title: Half a Humanity
chapters.summary: Beatrix decodes enough to learn the truth: Meridian's landing systems can only support waking half the colonists. Her mother built the dream to decide which half. Emotional beat: horror at inheriting a god's dilemma without godlike certainty.

chapters.title: The Criteria
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. The adults discover the children's dreams are changing their neural patterns — empathy heightened, aggression dulled. Some parents rejoice; others call it theft. Emotional beat: love for the children set against terror of what's being done to them.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: A faction aboard Meridian attempts to destroy the dream-link; the backlash surges down the beam and nearly kills Beatrix. Ilya keeps her conscious through the link. Emotional beat: first physical intimacy mediated entirely by signal — closeness without touch.

chapters.title: Elena's Testament
chapters.summary: Beatrix unlocks her mother's full testament: Elena chose the dreamers — those whose minds could hold both sleep and waking — believing love, not strength, should survive. Emotional beat: understanding without forgiveness; the inheritance revealed as a burden deliberately passed.

chapters.title: The Waking Vote
chapters.summary: Meridian's council demands the choice be put to a vote among the sleeping — impossible — or imposed by force. They order Beatrix to shut the beacon down. Emotional beat: duty tightening like a wire around everything she's begun to want.

chapters.title: Ninety-Six Hours
chapters.summary: Beatrix calculates the window: in four days Meridian enters the system, and whatever choice stands becomes permanent. Ilya proposes a third path neither fully understands yet. Emotional beat: urgency fused with hope, the clock now audible in every scene.

chapters.title: Descent Into the Sub-Basement
chapters.summary: Beatrix physically descends into the buried transmitter and finds Elena's body preserved at its heart, wired into the machine — the beacon runs on a mind. Emotional beat: revulsion and tenderness entwined; her mother never left, and never let go.

chapters.title: What Love Weighs
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. The council moves to forcibly wake the strong and abandon the dreamers, including the children. Ilya must choose between protecting the younger dreamers and trusting Beatrix's unproven plan. Emotional beat: loyalty tested, the cost of faith in another person.

chapters.title: The Rewriting
chapters.summary: Beatrix begins editing the beacon's broadcast — turning a selection algorithm into a translation layer, teaching sleeping minds to share the waking world's load. It works, barely, and burns out half the station. Emotional beat: creation as an act of defiance, brilliance shadowed by sacrifice.

chapters.title: Blackout
chapters.summary: With the station crippled, contact with Meridian goes silent during the final approach. Beatrix, injured and alone again, must trust that what she planted took root. Emotional beat: the deepest loneliness of the book — solitude chosen this time, and endured differently.

chapters.title: The Landing
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Meridian makes planetfall blind; the dreamers, still asleep, guide the waking pilots through shared vision. Half wake to soil and sky; half remain dreaming beneath the surface in vault-ships. Emotional beat: collective triumph shot through with irrevocable loss.

chapters.title: Two Kinds of Morning
chapters.summary: Beatrix crash-lands on the new world and walks out of the wreckage into a crowd of faces she only ever heard. Ilya finds her. Emotional beat: overwhelming arrival — belonging achieved after a lifetime of exile, almost too much to bear.

chapters.title: The Dreaming Vaults
chapters.summary: Beatrix visits the sleeper vaults and speaks to the dreaming half of humanity through the relay she rebuilt from wreckage. They answer — not as patients but as citizens. Emotional beat: reconciliation between halves, grief transmuted into stewardship.

chapters.title: Elena's Grave
chapters.summary: Beatrix returns to orbit one last time to shut down the old beacon and give her mother's body back to the dark. She reads Elena's final unencrypted line aloud: 'Forgive me the arithmetic.' Emotional beat: mourning completed, the debt of inheritance acknowledged and released.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: One year on. The waking colony thrives; the dreamers send images up every night like weather. Beatrix and Ilya, together now, teach the children to carry both worlds. Emotional beat: quiet joy, love that survived duty without defeating it.

chapters.title: Odile and the Colony
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, years later, writing the record that opens the book. She names the beacon Odile — the swan who was two things at once — and signs the log as technician, daughter, bridge. Final image: the settlement's lights below, the vaults' glow above, and her hand in Ilya's. Emotional beat: peace earned, identity claimed at last.
